Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq and his students: Abu Hanifa and Malik
hook: A gate of knowledge opened in Medina: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq and the scholars who came to his circle.
scenes.0.text: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq was born in Medina in 80 (699) or 83 (702); most sources take 83 as the basis. His father is Imam Muhammad al-Baqir, and his lineage reaches Imam Ali and Lady Fatima. His mother is Umm Farwa, the daughter of Qasim b. Muhammad; Qasim is a grandson of Abu Bakr. In the reports he is called the Sixth Imam, and in the reports a great scholar and a member of the Ahl al-Bayt. He is known by the epithet "al-Sadiq," the truthful.

Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq
scenes.1.text: His youth coincided with the years in which the Umayyad dynasty was unraveling. Then power passed to the Abbasids. Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq did not take part in the uprisings; in Medina he turned to knowledge and teaching. In the reports, Caliph al-Mansur had him poisoned. TDV relates this report as a Shia report.

scenes.2.text: Teaching circles were established around the Prophet's Mosque in Medina. The number of those who heard hadith from him is put as high as four thousand. Shaykh al-Mufid in al-Irshad, and Ibn Uqda in his work counting his students, mention four thousand people. In Shaykh al-Tusi's Rijal about 3,200 names appear. The figure varies from source to source. TDV too gives the number "according to Shia sources."
scenes.2.art.actors.0.label: 1ytn1vq
Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq
scenes.3.text: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq's learning is associated with hadith, jurisprudence and kalam. Because Shia jurisprudence rests on the reports of him and his father, it bears the name Ja'fari school. In the reports, the imams' knowledge is described as a trust that came from the Prophet. TDV mentions him, without regarding him as infallible, as a respected mujtahid. The attribution of chemistry and medicine is not sound. TDV considers the report that he passed knowledge to Jabir b. Hayyan highly doubtful; researchers such as Ruska and Kraus find it baseless. The medical Ihtilaj al-a'da' is attributed to him. Most of the works on chemistry and jafr may be products of later Shia-Batini circles.
scenes.3.art.actors.0.label: 1ytn1vq
Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq
scenes.4.text: His relationship with Abu Hanifa is a scholarly encounter. TDV writes that Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq held conversations with him in Medina and in Iraq. The entry on Abu Hanifa says that he met with Ahl al-Bayt scholars including Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq and benefited especially in matters of creed; it does not explicitly count Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq as his teacher. The main chain runs through Hammad b. Abi Sulayman, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and al-Sha'bi. In the reports, Abu Hanifa is mentioned as a student of Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq.

scenes.5.text: The saying "Had it not been for those two years, Nu'man would have perished" is attributed to Abu Hanifa. This saying shows how his relationship with Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq is remembered. The duration of the discipleship, however, is not known with certainty.

scenes.6.text: Malik b. Anas is mentioned among those who heard hadith from Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq in Medina. The teaching circles established in the same city left their mark on different schools of jurisprudence.

scenes.7.text: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq's learning reached beyond the teaching circle in Medina. Later generations remembered him for his accumulated knowledge in hadith and jurisprudence.

scenes.8.text: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq passed away in Medina in 148 H. (765) and was buried in Jannat al-Baqi'. He is the founder of the Ahl al-Bayt school and of the Ja'fari school; his circle of learning is regarded as the foundation of this school. In the reports he is mentioned as a respected circle of Medinan learning. This circle is a gate that both traditions mention in common.

sunni.0.says: Born 80/83, died 148 H, Medina. His mother Umm Farwa (daughter of Qasim b. Muhammad). Malik heard hadith from him, and he had scholarly debates with Abu Hanifa. His reports are in the Kutub al-Sitta, not in Bukhari's Sahih. The attribution of chemistry is highly doubtful.

disputes.0.title: wi5w1j
Was Abu Hanifa a student of Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq?
disputes.0.shia: The scholarly relationship between Abu Hanifa and Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq is mentioned in both sources. In the Shia account Abu Hanifa is his student; Ibn Abi al-Hadid also counts him as a student. An early source for the "two years" saying has not been found.
disputes.0.sunni: The scholarly relationship between Abu Hanifa and Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq is mentioned in both sources. TDV writes this as meeting and benefiting in creed, and does not describe him as a student; the "two years" saying is not in early sources.
disputes.1.title: 1ekxows
Did Malik narrate from Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq?
disputes.1.shia: That Malik heard hadith from Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq is mentioned in both sources. In the Shia transmission, this rests on the report of going to him in al-Saduq's al-Khisal.
disputes.1.sunni: That Malik heard hadith from Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq is mentioned in both sources. TDV writes this explicitly; the place and numbers in the Muwatta could not be verified in this study.
disputes.2.title: 14qgmss
Does the knowledge of chemistry and medicine belong to Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq?
disputes.2.shia: The attribution of some works to Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq is disputed on both sides. In later Shia-Batini circles certain books are tied to him; some works of Jabir b. Hayyan present themselves as an exposition of his teaching.
disputes.2.sunni: The attribution of some works to Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq is disputed on both sides. TDV considers the report that he passed knowledge to Jabir highly doubtful; Ruska and Kraus find it baseless. Only the medical work called Ihtilaj al-a'da' is attributed to him.
questions.0: TDV attributes the absence of reports from Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq in Bukhari's Sahih not to weakness but to fabricated hadith having been ascribed to his name. Why does it become harder to protect a name within a wide circle of learning?
questions.1: The figure of four thousand occurs in al-Mufid and Ibn Uqda, and about 3,200 in al-Tusi. How do large numbers of narrators let one read the breadth of a circle of learning?
questions.2: The "two years" saying cannot be found in early sources. Why does a saying's being famous not by itself show its historical record?
questions.3: In the unraveling of the Umayyads and the rise of the Abbasids, Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq chose teaching without entering into rebellion. What kind of guidance was keeping the circle of learning open in those years?
questions.4: Malik and Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq were formed in the same Medinan learning. As the boundaries of the schools are drawn, how can common teachers and common reports be remembered?
summary: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (d. 148 H) established an open circle of learning in Medina. That Malik heard hadith from him is also in TDV. His relationship with Abu Hanifa is described in Shia sources as discipleship and in TDV as a scholarly meeting. The Ja'fari school took shape through the reports of this circle.
key: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq and the school of learning
notes.0: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq was born in Medina in 83 H (702) and died there in 148 H (765).
notes.1: He did not take part in political uprisings; he turned to knowledge.
notes.2: The number of students is given as roughly between 3200 and 4000, depending on the source.
notes.3: Ja'fari jurisprudence is known by his name.
notes.4: That Malik heard hadith from him is in TDV; his relationship with Abu Hanifa is disputed.
